# Aesthetics {#ggplot2-aesthetics}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this matters

Aesthetics map variables to position, color, size and shape so patterns pop out.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Putting a constant inside aes() (e.g. aes(color='red')) creates a bogus legend; constants belong outside aes().
:::

In this chapter, we will focus on the aesthetics: color, shape, size, alpha,
line type and line width. We can map these to variables or specify values for
them. To map them to variables, we specify them within the `aes()` function. We
will look at both methods in the following sections.

Explore aesthetics such as 

- color
- shape
- size
- fill
- alpha
- width

```{r aes1, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
```

## Libraries, Code & Data

We will use the following libraries in this chapter:

- [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org/)
- [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/)
- [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/)
- [tidyr](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/)

All the data sets used in this chapter can be found [here](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets).

### Data

```{r import, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
ecom <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/web.csv')
ecom
```

### Data Dictionary

- id: row id
- referrer: referrer website/search engine
- device: device used to visit the website
- bouncers: whether the visit bounced (single page viewed)
- n_visit: number of visits
- n_pages: number of pages visited
- duration: time spent on the website (in seconds)
- country: country of origin
- purchase: whether visitor purchased
- order_items: number of items ordered
- order_value: order value of visitor (in dollars)

## Color

In ggplot2, `color` or `colour` usually refers to the color of the geoms. The
`fill` argument specifies the color of the shapes in certain cases. In this
first section, we will see how to specify the color for the different geoms we
learned in the previous chapter.

### Point

For points, the `color` argument specifies the color of the point for certain
shapes and the border for others. The `fill` argument specifies the background
for some shapes and does not work with others. Let us look at an example:

```{r aes2, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()
```

We can also map the variable to color in the `geom_point()` function, since it
inherits the data from `ggplot()`.

```{r aes3, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(cyl)))
```

If you do not want to map a variable to color, specify it separately using the
`color` argument, outside the `aes()` function.

```{r aes4, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = 'blue')
```

Now we will change the shape of the points to understand the difference between
the `color` and `fill` arguments. Shape can again be mapped to variables or
values. Let us map shape to variables.

```{r aes5, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg, shape = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()
```

Let us map shape to `cyl` in the `geom_point()` function. Remember, when you
map an aesthetic to a variable, it must be inside `aes()`.

```{r aes6, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = factor(cyl)))
```

Instead of mapping shape to a variable, let us specify a value for shape. In
this case, `shape` is outside `aes()` because we are not mapping it to a
variable.

```{r aes7, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape = 5)
```

Let us specify a color for the point using `color` argument.

```{r aes8, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape = 5, color = 'blue')
```

Not all shapes take a background color. In the example below, we try to modify
the background color using the `fill` argument but it does not work.

```{r aes9, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape = 5, fill = 'blue')
```

Since shapes 21–25 have both a fill and a border, the `fill` argument adds the
background color:

```{r aes10, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, fill = 'blue')
```

For shapes 21–25, the `color` argument will modify the border of the shape.

```{r aes11, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, color = 'blue')
```

Let us map the size of points to a variable. Map size only to continuous
variables, not categorical variables.

```{r aes12, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg, size = disp)) +
  geom_point()
```

To make every point the same size, set `size` outside `aes()`; the value is a
constant, not a variable.

```{r aes13, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(size = 4)
```

To modify the opacity of the color, use the `alpha` argument.

```{r aes14, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = factor(cyl)), color = 'blue')
```

## Line Chart

So far we have focused on `geom_point()` to learn how to map aesthetics to
variables. To explore line type and line width, we will use `geom_line()`. In
the previous chapter, we used it to build line charts. Now we will modify the
appearance of the line. In the section below, we will specify values for color,
line type and width. In the next section, we will map the same to variables in
the data. We will use a new data set, `EuStockMarkets`, a data set
that ships with R. It records the daily closing prices of four European stock
indices — DAX, SMI, CAC and FTSE — from mid-1991 to mid-1998. See
`?EuStockMarkets` for details and the source.

### Data

```{r import2a, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
stocks <- as.data.frame(EuStockMarkets)
stocks$year <- as.numeric(time(EuStockMarkets))
head(stocks)
```

We can create a line chart using `geom_line()`. In the example below, we
examine the DAX index and modify the color of the line to `'blue'`.

```{r aes15, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(color = 'blue')
```

To modify the line type, use the `linetype` argument. It can take values 
between 1 and 5. 

```{r aes16, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linetype = 2)
```

The line type can also be specified by name:

```{r aes17, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linetype = 'dashed')
```

Use the `linewidth` argument to modify the width of the line.

```{r aes18, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks, aes(year, DAX)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2)
```

Now let us map the aesthetics to the variables. We cannot use the data from the
example above, because we need a variable with index names. We will use the
`pivot_longer()` function from the `tidyr` package to reshape the data.

```{r aes19, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
stocks2 <-
  stocks |>
  select(year, DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -year, names_to = "index", values_to = "price")

head(stocks2)
```

To map the aesthetics to a variable, we must use the `group` argument. In the
example below, we map the aesthetics to `index`. But we cannot distinguish
between the lines, as their color, width and line type are the same. We have
easily plotted the price trend of all four indices using the `group` argument.
Now let us ensure that we can distinguish and identify them using different
aesthetics.

```{r aes20, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line()
```

Let us begin by giving the lines different colors with the `color` argument,
mapped to `index` inside `aes()`.

```{r aes21, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = index))
```

Instead of color, now we modify the line type using the `linetype` argument.

```{r aes22, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = index))
```

In the example below, we assign a different width to each line using the
`linewidth` argument.

```{r aes23, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(stocks2, aes(year, price, group = index)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = index))
```

Before we wrap up, let us quickly see how we can map aesthetics to variables 
for different plots.

## Bar Plots

Here we create a stacked bar plot by mapping `fill` to `purchase`.

```{r aes24, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(ecom, aes(device, fill = purchase)) +
  geom_bar()
```

## Histograms

Instead of a bar chart, we create a histogram and again map `fill` to 
`purchase`.

```{r aes25, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(duration, fill = purchase), bins = 10)
```

## Box Plots

We repeat the same exercise below, but replace the bar plot with a box plot.

```{r aes26, fig.align='center', fig.height=5, fig.width=6}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(device, duration, fill = purchase))
```

In all the cases above, you can observe that when we map aesthetics such as
color, fill, shape, size or linetype to variables, they are all wrapped inside
`aes()`.

## Exercises

1. Map `color` to cylinders and set a constant point `size = 3` outside `aes()`.
2. Map `linewidth` (not `size`) to a line geom and explain the difference.
3. Reshape a two-column wide table with `pivot_longer()` and map the key to color.
